item.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale (383 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification, See on Hacker News

Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal
Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich
Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

  • The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;
  • The exact theorem statements that were proved;
  • The Rocq proof checker itself.5

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.

Finding and fixing bugs

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.

Proving more than memory safety

Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.

Other formal verification case studies

Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.

We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA.7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. Along the way, we found some minor (unexploitable) bugs in corner cases, which are in the process of being filed upstream. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.

In another experiment, we asked Claude to develop an interpreter for a large subset of Python in Rust, and to prove (using Verus, a verification tool for Rust) that it adheres to the CPython semantics outlined in an academic paper. We then measured the adherence to CPython’s behavior empirically, running over 1.7 million randomly generated Python programs, finding identical behavior with CPython in 99.95% of tests, with remaining test differences as unsurprising known corner cases.

We also found issues in several widely used and critical applications via formal verification attempts of simple security properties. In one of them, we discovered a previously unknown logic bug that had been latent for more than a decade. During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, we found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported in a year.

See the Appendix for more details on some of these efforts.

This is just the beginning

One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve.

Newer models need fewer tokens

We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code. Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.

Proofs can be reused

When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.

We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6).

This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib, a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software).

As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language.

This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

Limitations

In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

“Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.

The claim may not cover everything we care about. We proved that a crash never triggers for any input under 64 MB on many fuzzing entry points in Google OSS-Fuzz, including ASan crashes. However, ASan doesn’t detect all memory safety bugs, and we didn’t verify all the entry points for each library. Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller. To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.

Conclusion

The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

item.title: Jared Kushner Hacked Phone Reveals Secret Negotiations, Millions in Transactions (460 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.vanityfair.com/story/jared-kushner-hacked-phone-secret-negotiations, See on Hacker News

An exclusive excerpt from Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East examines how bank accounts linked the president’s son-in-law—and former senior adviser—to Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.

In late spring 2020, a source I knew to be reliable called me with a story. The Dutch government had hacked into Jared Kushner’s phone and monitored him as he accessed a Dubai-based bank account. What was odd, the source said, was that the money in the account—hundreds of millions of dollars—had come from a bank in Azerbaijan. Most importantly, Kushner appeared to have transferred significant amounts of money from the Dubai account to other individuals, including a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man. The story sounded preposterous, I told my source. And yet.

Six months later, I found myself speaking with someone else about the UAE government and their use of mercenaries in conflicts around the Middle East and Africa when I asked, on a whim, whether they knew anything about Kushner and bank transfers from a UAE account. My acquaintance grew quiet. Then they replied, “Yes.”

Over the next four years, I came to learn that, sometime in late 2017, the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) made a startling discovery. A General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) operative, a dark web hacker specializing in stolen bank data, was traveling to the UK for an espionage mission. They reached out to the British government for permission to apprehend him when he arrived. The British agreed.

When the Russian national arrived in England, the Dutch informed him that he had two options: he could work for them against the GRU, or the British would arrest him. Once in UK government custody, the operative would be charged with espionage. If convicted, he would spend years in a British prison. The Russian chose to change his employer.

'Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East' by Matthew Cole

Later that year, the Russian operative gave the Dutch spies access to one of the GRU’s most sensitive assets. Located in Rostov, Russia, the GRU’s hacking and cyber team operated a remote server on which they stored some of their bounty. During their search through these secret files, the Dutch found something astonishing: screenshots of Jared Kushner’s iPhone.

In The Hague, the MIVD hacking team tried to reverse engineer the Russian penetration of Kushner’s iPhone. Kushner owned what was then the latest model, the iPhone X. Released in November 2017, it featured Face ID, a state-of-the-art security feature that Apple had promoted at its launch. The Dutch team had been trying to pick the phone’s door lock, so to speak, when it occurred to them that the Russians may have found an unlocked window to gain entry instead. Their hypothesis was correct. By early 2018, the MIVD had found a vulnerability in the iPhone that gave them access. The security exploit wasn’t perfect, however. Some malware allows a hacker to turn a victim’s phone into a microphone and video camera, turn the phone on or off, and pull and add files. The Dutch solution did not provide that level of access. Instead, when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner’s screen as he used it, filing their own cache of surveillance on their internal computer servers.

As they monitored Kushner’s phone, they discovered he used it to log in to a UAE bank account. By the time the Dutch spies had visibility into the phone, the account had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. Their initial assessment was that the bank account was affiliated with the government there.

For the MIVD hackers, the bank account became an intelligence mystery to unravel. Nearly everything they worked on had a tinge of Russian conspiracy. A little over a year into Trump’s first presidency, the MIVD, like FBI agents and federal prosecutors in Washington working on the Robert Mueller investigation, had only part of the story.

Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept. Despite the perception of his wealth, Kushner was not entirely financially independent of his parents, and the family business, Kushner Companies, faced a billion-dollar loan coming due on their trophy property, the Manhattan office building at 666 Fifth Avenue.

Early in the first Trump administration, MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals. The idea was to help pay for Trump’s promised wall between Mexico and the US, for example, in an effort to secure a second term in the White House. The two Arab royals initially discussed with Kushner putting more than $10 billion into the effort. Within months, though, as MBZ pushed the Trump administration to help back MBS’s effort to become his country’s crown prince—and future king—the broader foreign policy slush fund idea fizzled. Instead, MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2 billion into at least two bank accounts for Kushner. It is unclear how the royals organized their $2 billion in combined payments, but they effectively split the cost. For the purposes of explanation, it is best to understand where and how each bank account was controlled.

Bank account Alpha was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in the UAE, and was overseen by MBZ’s brother, Tahnoon bin Zayed, who served as the bank’s chairman. Beginning in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis transferred roughly $750 million into the Alpha account. Alpha would be used as a foreign policy fund. This money would be overseen and partially managed by Kushner and MBZ, who, in their effort to strike a grand bargain to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, believed the region’s map needed to be redrawn.

“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source who knew of the UAE’s deal with Kushner said. This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. “Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off.” A slush fund—a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives—was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption, this person explained. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”

The Alpha account looked like the funding source of a UAE government program, by which MBZ paid his bureaucrats their salaries or funded government-run schools. But how and through whom the money flowed into the Alpha account revealed that it was intended to remain secret, more akin to a covert and illicit scheme, given that it was managed in part by a senior advisor to the president of the United States.

The Dutch spies who monitored the Alpha account noted that all of it was sent by a bank in Azerbaijan in American dollars. Azerbaijan plays a unique role in money laundering. Its central bank maintains high levels of US dollars in its reserves but does not adhere to the highest standards of bank transparency. As a result, Azerbaijani banks have well-established but unadvertised practices of serving as way stations for large transfers, in which a foreign currency is exchanged for an equal amount in dollars. For a roughly 6 to 7 percent fee on the transaction, some Azerbaijani banks will accept a transfer from a client who wishes to move Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. The Saudi or Emirati client sends the money to the Azerbaijani bank, which then uses a different internal bank account to transfer the equivalent US dollars to the client’s requested destination. For auditors, this shadow trade can’t be discerned.

A shallow audit, as the Dutch tried while monitoring Kushner’s iPhone, revealed nothing more than what appeared to be an Azerbaijani government–linked bank account that sent hundreds of millions of dollars to an account in Dubai. But there was another aspect of the Alpha account that the Dutch couldn’t see or understand, one that helped reveal the secret purpose of the money. Kushner did not own the bank account at First Abu Dhabi Bank. He was a signatory for an account managed and owned by an Emirati charity.

When MBZ and MBS first began contributing to the Alpha account in 2017, the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a UAE government-funded charity, was run by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi. Al Falasi was a technocrat and a member of the Federal National Council, and friends with one of MBZ’s closest friends and advisors. As a result, Al Falasi and the Watani Foundation had a second mission. The charity was used as a cover to move money in support of the country’s secret military and intelligence operations overseas. Under the Watani cover, Al Falasi helped facilitate the UAE’s secret weapons-purchasing programs, one confidential source who had direct knowledge of the charity’s proliferation program revealed. This source said that the Emiratis believed that the program’s status as a charity made its international transactions less likely to be scrutinized and therefore served as a useful cover for funding MBZ and his brother’s secret wars.

MBZ and Tahnoon made Kushner a signatory on the Alpha account with Watani. As a signatory, Jared had access to it and could, in theory, make transactions, but it technically wasn’t his account. One way to view what Kushner did with the Alpha account is to imagine him as the director of the CIA. Had he been running the government entity that managed and ran secret foreign programs, maintaining the account, again, with presidential approval and congressional disclosure, Kushner’s conduct would have been within his job’s responsibilities. But he was not the director of the CIA, whose position is approved by the Senate and whose operations are overseen and accountable to Congress. Instead, Kushner was overseen only by his father-in-law, who, according to four senior Trump administration officials—two national security advisors, a White House chief of staff, and a former CIA director—were unaware of any presidential authorization for Kushner to access a foreign government bank account. (Kushner’s counsel, however, said Kushner did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed to by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.)

Regardless of whether he was a signatory or the owner, Jared was required by federal government regulations and the Internal Revenue Service to disclose his access to the account. Unless disclosed to and approved by the US government and reported on his tax returns, Kushner’s access to the Alpha account may have violated US law. (A lawyer for Mr. Kushner denied that his client had any knowledge of or connection to Al Falasi, the Watani charity, or a UAE bank account and stated that he had complied with all legal requirements when dealing with foreign governments.)

In addition to the Alpha bank account, MBZ put money into at least one other account intended for Kushner. By the spring of 2018, the crown prince had moved roughly $1 billion to Israel via Azerbaijan for Kushner. We will refer to this account as the Beta bank account. It is unclear how Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu first learned of MBZ’s money for Kushner, but a person briefed on the Beta account told me that the prime minister encouraged Kushner to have the money deposited in the Israeli Central Bank, in what would appear to be a government account. It is also unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him, but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit. But as with the Alpha account, there were clues in the way the Beta account was managed.

Israel’s Central Bank does not operate personal accounts. The bank holds and transfers only government funds. The government accounts use a dual-key system, which requires two authorized individuals to make any transfers from the account as an oversight mechanism. Netanyahu required Kushner to inform him before making any transactions from the Beta account.

To do so, Kushner passed his messages through Ambassador David M. Friedman, who frequently met with Netanyahu. With the money in the Central Bank, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to connect MBZ’s payment to Jared. It is unclear if spies in the Netherlands had any indication of the Beta account. (Ambassador Friedman denied that he had any knowledge of, or involvement with, any UAE money made available to Kushner, or that he passed messages on Kushner’s behalf. “I know absolutely nothing about any of these allegations,” Friedman said, “and the specific allegations about me or my alleged involvement in this alleged scheme are 100% false.” Kushner’s counsel also said Kushner “has no idea” about any such account, and insisted that “there are no accounts and never were.”)

Apparently, Kushner faced the challenge of moving money from the Beta account in Israel to other accounts where he could have untraceable access to the funds. One person who worked with Kushner to move the money out of Israel said that much of it went to bank accounts in Cyprus before being moved elsewhere.

During Kushner’s secret financial arrangement with MBZ, he helped negotiate a third, altogether distinct account. As part of what was, at the time, a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE, Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE from a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of the emergency defense, however, and the government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defense fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Although Kushner’s position as senior advisor to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosures for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House, he had to file both a public and confidential financial form, known as the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, also known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory—or beneficiary—access.

Kushner’s apparent betrayal of the public trust, however, went further than his failure to disclose the secret Alpha account in the UAE or the Beta account in Israel. By giving him access to roughly $2 billion, regardless of how the money was used, MBZ and MBS were paying for his influence within the US government. Any efforts he made to shape US policy that came from a foreign government that had provided him with money would make him an agent of a foreign power. US law requires citizens who lobby on behalf of a foreign power to declare themselves and the country they are working on behalf of to the Justice Department.

One former prosecutor who worked on the Mueller investigation said that if Kushner promised anything to MBZ and MBS in return for the money they offered him—even if it was just speaking to his father-in-law—he may have violated federal bribery laws, as well as the foreign agent statute. (Mr. Kushner’s lawyer denied that Kushner violated any laws while serving in the White House.)

item.title: HNInternal: Ask HN: If the models are so good, why doesn't OpenAI just start 100 companies? (286 pts)
item.description:
See on Hacker News


That would scare people away from sharing their knowledgebases with them and regulators to act. At this stage, as long as people are sharing more and more knowledge with the models or if there is roadmap to collect more training data somehow, the smart move is to wait.

But look at the ArtCraft project. At least one of labs has an internal benchmark to clone 20+ popular products much like ArtCraft but with much higher budget and several configurations of the workflow. ArtCraft spent $20K initially, not sure how much by now, but they are moving fast and the apps work. They day is coming when they can flip and just clone everything including the ops.


1. They are starting to do it. Take a look at OpenAI's product portfolio, there's a galaxy of attempts at application.

2. Selling tokens via long running agents is the only thing that's provably working with respect to revenue growth.

3. They need revenue yesterday. Increases in borrowing rates means access to capital isn't what it was in the 10s. Their runway is much shorter than you would imagine.

4. Some of the decision makers at these companies believe AI will exhibit Jevons Paradox and that any decrease in price will result in induced demand.

5. The frontier models are still subject to the limitations of AI. They're not good at everything. Better to have someone else learn that on their dime rather than yours.


3 is biggest point imo.

Openai haven't yet amortised their current investments into the space and nor have they stopped making new ones.

I'm sure they'd be totally capable of bringing 1k new biz online but that's even more debt, and even more uncertainty.


Some variation(s) of 5 is carrying a lot of weight. Need a person with an Idea. Need someone to refine their idea. Need someone to spend the time filtering through the slop to find the good bits. Much better to sell people on the idea of their dream being created while you sell them tokens to do that.

That all said, A person trusting the big AI companies with their golden goose idea seed leaves a lot of concerning openings down the road if that idea gets "leaked" out to others. Similar concern of mine with if the LLM outputs that made your idea happen to be reused by the big company if someone else asks similar enough questions or otherwise coaxes the AI to reveal what it did for you.

All this AI generation is gonna be a lead to a wild time for IP law.


>3. They need revenue yesterday. Increases in borrowing rates means access to capital isn't what it was in the 10s

This is a huge problem, why is it like this


they've borrowed so much they're directly competing with national governments in capital markets.


OpenAI has hardly borrowed anything. They have a $4B revolving credit line but have hardly touched it. They haven't issued any bonds.

Investment isn't debt.


The rates environment directly dictates what capital is available to OpenAI and at what terms. When potential investors can get x% virtually guaranteed, then they are less willing to give cash for equity to OpenAI.


Investment isn’t debt, but investment and debt demand revenue in functionally identical ways, and OpenAI has taken an enormous amount of investment, so they are subject to broadly the same pressures as a hypothetical company that had borrowed lots, no?


Isn't investment like a form of debt, or well obligation to make returns?

If VC provide you funds, there is an expectation of returns, otherwise the board would vote you out.

Yeah it's not a traditional loan from a bank, but it's not a 0% interest loan either.


The duopoly AI labs haven't technically borrowed much, but a metric ass-ton of money has been borrowed by various other entities in service of them as infrastructure proxies.

That's what is driving up the cost of debt and teetering some of these companies into junk status.


Well, they've certainly moved up the application stack already. There is no doubt that they'll keep doing that while deploying services through deploy.co and ode.com.

Some 15 years ago people would say "Why would crypto miners even sell you hardware? Why not just keep it for themselves and mine the crypto?" and then it turned out that after you paid for a device you'd often get it slightly used with the cryptocurrency going to the hardware miner. The models are unbelievably good.


they would need to literally build a 1000 unicorns to make an impact on their valuation. Or a million small companies - at which level surely even american antitrust agency would begin to look at them.

Also, it would increase anti AI sentiments, and people’s fears of then using private data - that’s the real cost.

In general you want to be careful about competing with your own clients.


Because they already employ thousands of programmers that the AI cannot replace. Don't believe the marketing hype about AGI, we are extremely far from it.


Going up the value chain is much more difficult as opposed to going down. A packaging company for example will have a much harder time creating a snack company than the snack company creating a packaging company. The snack company will know exactly what it needs for its packaging and have strict requirements.

Down the chain you see what you need to do because you work directly with it everyday.


This is more or less the same as a question Alex Karp asked in that hilariously off-the-rails CNBC interview: why, if the code is so good, are they selling by the token and not asking for a cut?

https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/tv/articles/televised-ne...

I think OpenAI actually will ultimately start a fleet of consultancy/SaaS spinoff companies, each perhaps short-lived until the core product does the job out of the box.


This is the central plot in the “Life 3.0” book that came out a few years ago.

[SPOILER] After the singularity, AI is able to dominate all markets – starting by gaming and entertainment – in order to generate cash to rent more servers to improve itself.


Imagine the Earth is covered in a "Grey Goo" outbreak of spreading nanotechnology, infiltrating every corner of the planet in a constant churn of molecular and informational warfare. Eventually it leads to vast colonies of nanobots which rise thousands of units high clambering across the land, driven by vast inscrutable colony-minds.

I can tell you with 100% certainty that they will pay rent, because they are us.


Being one of the premiere AI companies is much more exciting to investors than "running a company using AI" which everyone can do


I agree, OpenAI is one of the leaders of the industry and the vision they have sold to investors of the great advancement of the human race is why they are valued at 852bn. Though most outlets and statistics say they are not making a profit, it's also just more axiomatic that OpenAI would focus on their firm's core business which is AI. Building another 100 companies is futile for them, though a little diversification can be advantageous.


They are doing that. That is why they have moved into the app layer. They are counting on software being replaced with agentic super apps. The only reason they aren’t starting actual service companies is that those still require human boots on the ground. But they are pushing their way into consulting (they bought my friends consulting firm)


It's basically the same reason why Apple didn't create every app in the App Store. No single company can be specialised in everything, and more importantly, selling tokens is risk-free money since they get a cut for every app without taking any business risk.


I think that’s a different argument. Apple absolutely “copies” hugely successful, durable apps. Just read about “getting sherlocked”. The rest of the apps are transient, niche and it’s easier to just harvest your cut of ads/payments.


Fair point about Sherlocking, but that's actually proves the analogy. Apple only "Sherlocks" broad, consumer-facing features, but they never touch specialised B2B or super niche software. AI model providers are doing the same thing. They build the broad stuff themselves, like AI inside Excel or PowerPoint, but they live the crazy stuff to other companies.


I wonder what is stopping apple from cloning the top ten apps in each category using AI and then booting the original developers off the app store.


> No single company can be specialised in everything

Not everything, but a company can be specialized in a lot of different things, Samsung for example, or megacorp in Japan.


Yeah, actually trying to specialize in everything constraints the firm's growth. Though diversifying can always bring some much-needed revenue like you said with Samsung or Tata in India.


Or amazon that can undercut any merchant on their platform by cross financing the losses by selling more aws servers.

That’s the other side of diversification: undercutting your competition until they go out of business. Then prices are raised again.


Yeah Amazon is another example I mean they do a lot of things too. AWS has changed software and Amazon prime which is a vehement competitor to Netflix and disney+ market share.


I believe this is the correct answer. You can't run 100 businesses because each one would only receive 1/100 of your attention, and they would all perform poorly.


But that’s the gist of the question, can’t their internal frontier models provide that infinite attention? That is what their PR implies.


I thought the agents were largely autonomous, and should replace workers?

If labor is not your constraint, you wouldn't be diverting your specialization.


Entrepreneurship 101 imo is that great companies only come from people who sufficiently care to see something through.

Unlikely the people that start these 100 companies, across totally disparate fields, and care enough to take them to market are staff members at OpenAI.

And it's already obvious a single company can't split its attention enough to do tons of disparate things well (see OpenAI's previous attempts at Atlas, the social network, Dots, etc)


There was/is a youtube commericial I think that gave away the game to some extent with regards to this. It was selling some platform to create apps. Everybody in the office rejoicing because they were all creating apps. Inevitably, like three people in the office make the same app.

I've experienced the same thing in real life a couple of times over.

I think Einstein's quote "A new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive and move toward higher levels." is apt. Apps will solve a bunch of problems, but if anyone can create those apps, there will be no market for them. I don't have the answers, but long term, it probably doesn't lie in selling apps. We've only just started.

At my regular job, we're just catching up on all the internal work we had. I think there is a real crunch in trying to figure out how to build moats and things that are hard to replicate that are sellable.

Maybe it will be the physical. Probably most of the moat will be made up of network effects and capital intensive processes. If I had the answer I'd probably be working on it right now.


But LLMs can do that now? Surely you could only have one or a few people managing everything with them. Or just have them build code that fully automates also that. After all software should be solved issue. So no point of not automating software for all aspects needed and then letting LLMs handle the rest.


1. Anything that can be easily done with an LLM can be done by anyone easily. Given that, the value of those things therefore drops to near zero.

2. All remaining things are at least as hard to do as before, but you may have removed some load from people that previously were more busy doing things from the (1) category manually. So these might drop in value a bit as there are more hours available with the existing people to do those.

3. Then, there are things that become harder because somebody used an LLM to do them. Imagine you have a project lead who didn't do one bit themselves, generated a bunch of specs and tickets using AI and handed them to you. You are the first one looking at them manually and you find out that they are garbage. Now, in all likelihood you have lost efficiency. This in my experience applies to all types of work that yield results which are hard to verify.

Which of those cancels out the other and what kind of feedback effect arises and what overall effect on productivity/efficiency this has, nobody knows.


Because running 1 business is easier than running 100 businesses. It takes a lot more than writing good software for a company to be successful.


You can just restate the question then to say: If the models are so good, why can't they run a business?


What does "so good" mean? AI models are very good at doing [a set of things]. Autonomously running a large, complex business is not one of them.


Bad argument.

Why go into the hamburger business when you think you've got an infinite profitability recipe on your hand potentially. The big AI houses have doubled down and quadrupled down on their core founding myth for better or worse.

The AI boom is a full send. Either this works in spectacular fashion or it blows in spectacular fashion.


The standard analogy is selling shovels, not hamburgers.

OpenAI is selling people access to a tool to build things. OP is asking why they don’t just build the things themselves, which I believe is a fair question.


The bet here is that it's not selling shovels but rather magic.

...a dubious proposition except this time there is a small but real chance it may be actual magic


I've heard this argument for AGI or SI. If the model gets smart enough then they won't have to sell inference, they can make money by doing any valuable thing.


Well they ARE.

Except they're called products - you don't open a new company for every new product you make.

And you don't make 100 - you focus the resources you have to try to build the most impactful things you can.


It's very simple: because it is not working and it brings risk.

You can't fail software project you don't start. But if you can sell tokens to company that fails, that's just profit for you!

LLMs aren't good enough to do project from start (and I mean actual start - getting requirements, figuring out the market etc.) to end. Hell it apparently isn't even good enough to run simple web store (even if it can write one).

It is a great multiplier for people that already know what they want to do, so they are selling to them.


Selling tokens in conjunction with a phone number or credit card yields signals for surveillance for intelligence agencies that can be tied to individuals. This keeps the firms relatively out of trouble with the federal government. This makes them too big to fail. Being subject to such surveillance is in fact is a strong reason for conscious individuals to seek to move away from them in the long term once the quality of competing AIs reaches a shared plateau.

They're doing the other thing too via numerous startup acquisitions.


This fits, if NVidia fully believed in the LLMs/AGI future, why would they waste their super valuable GPUs by selling them? Why not just make your own LLM with the advantage of being one of the few major compute providers?


Nvidia already does that, their models just aren't competitive.

Google is doing it successfully to the point where they only let you rent their shovels and never let you buy them.


Yeah, but I also don't think it's that deep. E.g., by the same line of thinking, TSMC should be doing what Nvidia / Apple / AMD are doing, and ASML what TSMC is doing.

NVidia is good at making the shovels, and sticks to that.


It’s not, but for fun I think that depends on if you see the models as just another technology or as a “country of geniuses in a datacenter”. The former means NVidia believes LLMs are fundamentally limited, and if that’s the case OpenAi and Anthropic are basically screwed as their core products become commodities.


There's some kind of skill needed in an organization to make those llms. Openai and anthropic were able too. The other llm creators, not really. There's no guarantee that Nvidia would be another leader and not end up like meta or xai's attempt


Deepseek claims to be making $38/gpu/hr on deepseek 4.1 flash, and I would say that’s probably marginally close to the frontier, so they don’t have to be as good as OpenAI/Anthropic. Even at half that revenue, NVidia makes back the cost of a b200 cluster in roughly half a year. (19*8*24*5*52 = 948,480)

It’s estimated NVidia sold 4.5-5.2 million gpus in 2025 with total revenue numbers at about $130b.

With this terrible math in mind, they could produce half of that and make substantially more money, basically an infinite money glitch.


Gold is much more fungible than a business. 100 different businesses are much more unique than 100 different gold nuggets.

The counter-argument is that the models might make business ideas just as fungible as anything else.


I think that the generative ui and self evolving databases per user is definitely coming, I think they are making this wager too. A lot of pieces of the ecosystem haven't been thought out fully yet and there is a shift in user experience e.g. a lot of people are more content with just using Dots then loading up apps and visuals, when they can just read what they needed to know.


Good point, instead of wasting their compute in solving 100 years old math problems.

Spoiler alert: it's a sarcasm


For what it’s worth, they are doing that in limited areas. For example the Figma/Claude design controversy.

But you are right, building a business is a lot more than building a product. It’s also a lot more than just name recognition because they have no shortage of that either.


In addition to what everyone’s saying about platform economics, the other big advantage of selling tokens to everyone rather than competing with them directly is that they get to see everyone’s tokens (and, with consent, train on them)


Because they want to be a platform for others to thrive. You make a lot more money when you are a successful platform than when you are a hundred successful products. That’s why Apple never made an iPhone for dentists.


Why would they try to run a real business when they can publish blogs about how spooky the product is and then live out the plot of the 1994 film Blank Check


I mean it sounds stupid but I think its a fair question if you can spend 15 million and solve a millennium prize problem, what happens if you take the same resources and just aim the cannon at making money?


First, two things can be true: the models can be amazingly good, and they can also be insufficient to run a company, at least now and maybe forever, because they are not "intelligent" in all the ways we are.

IMO the invention of AI is redefining what we think of as "intelligence". You would probably describe Albert Einstein as highly intelligent, and you'd probably also describe Bill Clinton as highly intelligent. Even before AI, you can easily look at that and see we aren't describing the same things even though we're using the same word. Einstein's intelligence is highly abstract, observational, mathematical. Clinton's is interpersonal, pursuasive, articulate, etc.

The AI we have today is extremely good at intellectual tasks like Einstein. It is not good at social intelligence and social agency like Clinton. Also, before you say that they can be really empathetic, persuasive, people are already socially dependent on them etc, that's not what I'm talking about. They are extremely knowledgeable about human socialising, but they cannot actually perform it. You could not set an AI out into the world to go and make a few friends.

I think the key moment will be if a single AI can get more than one person to care about what it has to say and what it's doing. Think about today how when someone tells you about their conversation with their AI agent, you probably roll your eyes because who cares, it's a highly individual experience.

Companies need a lot of this. They have to form relationships, become trusted amongst society, etc. AI cannot do this right now, and it's increasingly clear "intelligence" is not sufficient to do it, at least not in the way LLMs are intelligent. Maybe one day they will, but I'd imagine that will be another enormous leap in what AI even looks like akin to how ChatGPT was an enormous leap.


During a gold rush, sell shovels. They are investing heavily in in-house custom silicon, which is the shovel end of things. They could open more jewellery chains, but that is a very different kind of operation and it is in their interest to let others compete for that and use their resources on the shovel side of things.

item.title: Hedra is a 3D open world game I wrote from scratch while in highschool (221 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/maxilevi/project-hedra/tree/pre-ai, See on Hacker News

Project Hedra is an ambitious open-world, low-poly RPG. Choose your class, explore endless procedurally generated worlds, unlock different skills and complete procedurally generated quests.

More screenshots at (Screenshots)

Timeline/Context

I started this project when I was in highschool (around 15 yo) in order to learn how OpenGL worked.

The scope creep quickly arrived and after a few years it turned into a fullfledged 3D game and game engine. The codebase has around 100k LOC and the game has first class support for Linux and Windows.

Features

The million lines of code are not in vain. The game and engine are both full of features :)

Game Features

  • Beatiful procedurally generated worlds
  • Quests and bosses
  • 100+ items with rarities system
  • Skills and skill tree system with N+ skills
  • 4 different classes with 2 specializations each ()
  • Procedurally placed structures generated dynamically
  • Fishing, crafting, etc
  • Trading and NPCs
  • Companions and pets
  • Beatiful soundtrack
  • Navigation, maps
  • Different dimensions
  • More stuff I don't recall :)

Engine Features

  • Fully fledged renderer using modern OpenGL
  • Skinned mesh rendering
  • Support for loading and playing generic animations
  • Collada (.dae) parser
  • Static mesh rendering
  • Screen space reflections
  • Screen space ambient occlusion
  • Bloom, FXAA & MSAA
  • Modding support
  • CI for automatically deploying to a Steam beta branch
  • Localization support
  • Sound support using OpenAL
  • Python scripting support
  • Module system for loading data oriented objects
  • Steam integration
  • Fully fledged UI & controls system (dropdowns, buttons, etc.) written from raw OpenGL
  • Dynamic shader system for reloading during runtime
  • Frustum culling, occlusion culling,
  • Mesh simplification for runtime level of detail (LOD)
  • Skybox support
  • Shadows
  • 3D trails renderering support
  • Particle system using object instancing in opengl
  • bulletphysics integration
  • Chunk system for infinite worlds support
  • .ply parsing support
  • Dynamic meshing support using MarchingCubes
  • Custom implementation of basic C# primitives and allocators (like Lists) for supporting stack allocated lists and minimizing the automatic runtime allocations (and thus the GC).
  • 1000+ plus test cases
  • Framework for mocking game components and doing integration testing on games
  • Image and asset compression for faster loading and smaller size
  • Entity component system
  • More stuff I don't recall :)

Interesting bits

  • WorldRenderer.cs. Renders the entire world in just 3 (actually it depends on how partitioned is the data buffer, but it was designed to be in 3) draw calls (water, terrain, instanced) using glMultiDrawElements.

  • Block.cs. Core component of the world. Read more at https://maxilevi.com/blog/procedural-meshing-hedra

  • Fishing.py. Written in Python as a mod script using IronPython, directly interacts with the C# API.

  • NativeArray.cs Implementation of an array primitive using a custom allocator. The same project provides heap based allocators as well as stac based ones using stackalloc. The idea was to minimize the automatic heap allocations (and thus avoiding the GC) during the game frames.

Interesting facts

  • The world is fully procedurally generated, there is no world save file. Only the player contents are saved and the world seed. The rest is created at runtime.
  • The world is voxel based but an isosurface extraction algorithm called Marching Cubes is applied to extract an implicit continous surface from the discrete voxels.
  • The name "Hedra" comes from tetrahedra which is the shape used in the original iso surface extraction algorithm I implemented Marching Tetrahedra
  • The game only supports loading .PLY and .DAE models, both which are in plaintext and the models have no textures. Therefore if you put this into perspective, this means I wrote a bunch of text that reads text and creates interactive images from this. I think this is pretty cool.

Screenshots

TODO add more

Code Structure

Overall Architecture

The game is a mod to a base engine. The idea of architecturing this way was to force myself to maintain the mod API up to date, therefore encouraging access to make mods.

Hedra

Basically the entire game. This includes AI logic, components, world generation, module systems, object placement and lots of other stuff.

Hedra.Engine

The core parts of the engine, this defines all the abstractions to the world. It handles rendering, sound, different base systems as well as the general windowing, game loop and platform features. The split was not done at the start so some stuff might still be outside.

Framework

Core primitives used in the engine. This includes heap and stack allocators, custom implementations of lists and arrays as well as wrappers to pointers to native and some other useful primitives

HedraTests

Test suite that

Asset Builder

Command line tool to compress the game assets into convenient binary files. Combines images, models, sound files, shaders into a single binary file with a structure designed for fast data retrieval.

Server

Once upong a time Hedra used to support multiplayer. It worked by doing UDP Hole Punching and having clients communicate P2P, this server was in charge of that. You might also see some networking remnants in the Engine code.

How to build

The build process is pretty straightforward.

  1. Checkout all the submodules
  2. Run the build depedencies scripts
  3. Compile the C# solution

You can check the GitHub actions workflows for some examples on Linux and Windows.

item.title: AI and the Enclosure of the Scientific Commons (136 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27251, See on Hacker News

Authors:P. K. G. Williams (Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian)

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.

item.title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents (436 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell, See on Hacker News

Important

New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide.

OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it.

How It Works

OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied.

  • Kernel-level enforcement. Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox. Kernel controls confine which files it can access and which system calls it can make, and every network connection passes through a policy check before it leaves the sandbox. Agents never see real credentials; OpenShell adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints.
  • Formally verified policy changes. Before a policy change is approved, OpenShell uses formal verification to flag risky new access it would grant, such as reaching a new host with credentials or calling a new API method, so those changes wait for human review.

See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together.

Quickstart

You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details.

curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh
openshell sandbox create --name demo

The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent: it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it.

Explore Further

  • Sandboxes: images, runtimes, GPUs, and lifecycle.
  • Policies: filesystem, network, and process rules, with the advisor and prover for reviewing changes.
  • Providers: credentials that work only at approved endpoints, including inference.
  • Gateways: the control plane for sandboxes, policy, and access.
  • Kubernetes: deploy the gateway with Helm. Your CNI must enforce NetworkPolicy.
  • Extensibility: middleware, interceptors, and compute drivers.
  • Tutorials: step-by-step policy and agent walkthroughs.
  • Prerelease and development builds: try an upcoming release or the latest commit on main.

Agent Skills

Install the public OpenShell skills for your coding agent:

npx skills add NVIDIA/OpenShell

The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout.

SDKs

SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible.

Language Install Docs
Python uv add openshell README
TypeScript npm install @nvidia/openshell-sdk (GitHub Packages) README
Go go get github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go@latest README
Rust cargo add openshell-sdk --git https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell --tag <release-tag> Installation and usage

Community

  • Questions and discussion: GitHub Discussions
  • Bug reports and feature requests: GitHub Issues, using the issue templates
  • Security vulnerabilities: follow SECURITY.md. Do not open a GitHub issue.
  • Roadmap: OpenShell Roadmap and the RFC board
  • Try it in the cloud: Brev Launchable

OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions.

Telemetry

OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely.
