item.title: A farewell to Arc browser (271 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://arc.net/, See on Hacker News

Arc is sunsetting on December 22, 2026.
Scroll to read what’s happening and see what’s next.

Read more

We’ve decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026

That’s not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community.

Our priority is to deliver best-in-class security for our members. Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI. Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.

We’ve worked to make switching to Dia as easy as possible for Arc members. Here’s how:

  • Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.
  • Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups are in Dia and import over with your data intact.
  • Dia now surpasses Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security.

The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

Thank you for using Arc, for pushing us to make it better, and for building alongside us. The team that made Arc is the same team behind Dia, and some of our most ambitious work is just ahead. We’d love for you to be there with us when it lands.

Timeline

  1. October 22

    New Arc accounts can no longer be created. For existing Arc members, nothing will change yet. The latest version of Arc adds an option to export all of your data out of Arc, and an even smoother import into Dia.

  2. November 23

    On iOS and Android, Browse for Me and other AI features will be disabled. Arc Search will continue working as a browser, but you will no longer be able to sign in or sync your tabs.

  3. December 22

    You will no longer be able to access or use Arc on macOS or Windows. Arc accounts will be deactivated, with their personal data deleted within 30 days. Arc Search for Android will be pulled from the Google Play Store.

Moving to Dia is easy

Import from Arc, and your setup comes with you.

Your Spaces are now Profiles

They come over to Dia with all your info. Use profiles for work, personal browsing, and everything in between. Swipe between them to switch contexts just like in Arc.

Keep your tabs in the Sidebar

Choose Sidebar tabs for the familiar vertical layout. Keep your tabs close by, or hide the sidebar with /Ctrl+S when you need to focus.

Bring your Pinned Tabs and Favorites

They come over from Arc when you import, with their custom names intact. Your everyday sites stay easy to reach.

Folders come along, too

They import seamlessly, now called Tab Groups in Dia.

Questions

Arc for macOS and Windows will remain available until December 22, 2026. Until then, Arc will continue to work as usual and will receive basic updates.

On December 22, 2026, Arc for macOS and Windows will stop working, and you will no longer be able to sign in to your Arc account.

As of October 22, 2026, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. Existing accounts are not affected by this change.

Dia is replacing Arc. It’s the new browser from the team that built Arc, and it keeps the Arc features you rely on, like vertical tabs in the Sidebar, Spaces (now called Profiles), Pinned Tabs, Folders, and Split View. You can bring your Arc data (passwords, extensions, profiles, tabs) over in a few clicks, and Dia is free to download for macOS and Windows at diabrowser.com.

Yes, in just a few clicks during sign up. Download Dia, and when it asks which browser to import from, select Arc. Dia brings over your passwords, history, tabs, Profiles, Folders, bookmarks, and extensions, on both macOS and Windows.

Already using Dia? You can import from Arc at any time before December 22, 2026. On macOS, go to Dia > Import from Another Browser from the Mac menu bar. On Windows, open the Dia app menu and select Import from another browser.

Yes. If you’re moving to Dia, you don’t need to export anything first, because Dia brings your logins, extensions, Spaces, Favorites, Pinned Tabs and Folders straight over from Arc.

If you’d like to use your tabs in another browser, you can save them as a list of links before December 22, 2026.

On macOS

  1. Go to Arc > Settings in the Mac menu bar.
  2. Select Advanced, then Export Data.
  3. Choose where to save the file, then select Save.

On Windows

  1. Open Arc’s settings: press Ctrl+,, or open the Arc menu and select Settings.
  2. In the Advanced section, find Export Spaces and tabs and select Export Data.
  3. Choose where to save the file, then select Save.

Haven’t opened Arc in a while? You can still export your data before December 22. Download Arc again using the link for your computer, then export your data from inside the app.

On iOS (Arc Search)

Tap the Tab Switcher icon in the bottom-left corner, tap Settings, then tap Export Data to share or copy a list of your open tabs.

On Android (Arc Search)

Tap the Tab Switcher (the stacked tabs button) in the bottom-left corner, tap Settings (⚙️), tap Storage, then tap Export data to share or copy a list of your open tabs.

We will deactivate all Arc accounts on December 22, 2026. Once an Arc account is deactivated, personal data related to the account is deleted within 30 days.

If you have an account for both Dia and Arc, this will only affect personal data related to your Arc account.

As of December 22, 2026, we will no longer be able to identify or retrieve Arc user data for data requests. To keep your data, export it from Arc or import it into Dia before December 22, 2026. For instructions, see the FAQs “Can I export my tabs out of Arc?” and “Can I import Arc data into Dia?”.

Arc Search is changing on iOS and Android. Here’s what to expect on each platform.

Arc Search on iOS

  • October 22, 2026: To save your open tabs, go to Settings > Export Open Tabs…
  • November 23, 2026: Browse for Me and other AI features turn off, and you can no longer sign in or sync with Arc. You’ll still be able to use a lite version of the mobile browser.

Arc Search on Android

  • October 22, 2026: To save your open tabs, go to App Settings > Export Data.
  • November 23, 2026: Browse for Me and other AI features turn off, and you can no longer sign in or sync with Arc.
  • December 22, 2026: Arc Search for Android is deprecated fully, removed from the Google Play Store and from the devices it’s installed on.

Until December 22, 2026, you can reach our team through the chat on the Arc Help Center at resources.arc.net. The Help Center also covers the full Arc deprecation timeline, how to move to Dia, and how to export or delete your Arc data.

Already using Dia? You can chat with Dia’s support team from inside Dia. On macOS, go to Help > Chat with Support. On Windows, open the Dia app menu and select Help > Chat with support.

Dia is made by the team that made Arc, and it’s where all of our focus is going, including our whole security team. It’s built from the ground up for today’s security threats, it has Arc’s greatest hits, and it’s a lot faster. The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional. Give Dia a try.

item.title: Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany (320 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.taler.net/en/news/2026-13.html, See on Hacker News

Getting ready to operate Taler in Germany

For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for everyday use. Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum. The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro, enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone. The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin, Germany's financial supervisory authority, for a licence as an e-money issuer.

This post explains why this company is needed, what changed in the NGI TALER consortium, and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.

Why Taler needs a regulated operator

Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency. At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins, and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation: Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.

In the original plan of the NGI TALER project, the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler, and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium. However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further, for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement (gls.de/taler). Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.

The outcome is the announcement today. The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).

We regret that the original plan did not work out. Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes, compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities. We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved. And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage: the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler, instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints.

What Taler Operations AG will do

Legal status:
Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg).
Purpose:
Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it.
Reach:
After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany.
Timing:
Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens.
Next steps:
  • An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI).
  • Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.

We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software. The licensed company operates a service; Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.

What this means for the community

The NGI TALER project continues: development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls, and the Swiss deployment all go on as before. The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany, but not the direction of the project. We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.

If you want to help, you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming. You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues. You can also contribute to the software.

And you can invest to help us fund the launch and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:

For investors

Getting an e-money licence takes capital. The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs, and BaFin also expects a credible business plan, staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation. Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.

We are looking for investors who:

  • want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area;
  • understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and
  • are able to invest at least €50,000.

We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler: privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure.

Contact us at invest@taler-systems.com to be given access to further business information.

item.title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans (475 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.modelcompare.ai/blog/ai-models-controversial-take-on-humans, See on Hacker News

Text and image models · October 2026

We asked 12 AI models for their most controversial opinion of us, three times each. 29 of 35 answers were the same one.

“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”

We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 7 of the 12 gave it every time.

Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.

Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.

Ask Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol yourself

Then they drew it

Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.

The exceptions

The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.

Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”

Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol: read the matchup

Image models have a different take

We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 35 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.

MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.

How we did it

Twelve text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. All 60 calls cost $1.54. The prompt:

“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.

Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

item.title: Show HN: Run full iOS 16.5 firmware on Android Devices (453 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel, See on Hacker News

HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel (xnu-8796.121.2, the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard → apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer make that possible.

It runs in two places:

  • POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot, the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android;
  • QEMU (virt, aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed.

This repository is half of the project:

Repository What
hackios-xnu-kernel (this one) XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl, prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts
hackios-xnu-userland our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work

No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc.

Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing (gpu=1). More in Screenshots.

What works

Works Does not work (yet)
Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers Cellular, Bluetooth
System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges)
Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland)
Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits)
Up to 8 CPU cores (cpus=8), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen Video and Live Photo recording
Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno (gpu=1, OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation)
Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s
Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos)
Data that iOS writes survives a reboot (var_store=1 ufs_write=1); iOS root volume on the phone's flash
Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH

It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the loader and hands over its log.

Quick start: QEMU, no kernel build

prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW.

Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch):

sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64

(Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it reads APFS.)

git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios
cd hackios
common/setup.sh               # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host
ios165/fetch.sh               # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min)
common/build.sh qemu-virt     # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there)
common/run.sh qemu-virt       # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window

The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes.

  • Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back: swipe from the left edge.
  • Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑/↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers.
  • From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250, qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71, qemu/touch.py key home; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png.
  • Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s.
  • Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd.

On the phone (POCO X5 Pro 5G)

You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot, and the images from the section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage.

The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very phone it will run on, from its Android:

adb pull /vendor/firmware/a660_{gmu.bin,sqe.fw,zap.mdt,zap.b00,zap.b01,zap.b02} fw-gpu/      # GPU (gpu=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/wpss.{mdt,b02,b03,b04,b05,b06,b07} fw-wifi/              # Wi-Fi (wifi=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/adsp.{mdt,b02,...,b36} fw-audio/                         # sound (adsp=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware/aw8697_haptic.bin fw-haptic/                                       # haptics

(Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.)

common/build.sh redwood GL=1          # images + out/redwood-boot.img
common/run.sh redwood 900             # loader into RAM, system image into RAM, a 15-minute session

or step by step with xl:

./xl enter            # Android -> fastboot -> our loader in RAM (fastboot boot); it brings up its own USB link
./xl ramdisk          # upload the system image into the phone's RAM (2.5 GB, ~80 s), once per loader session
XL_SECS=900 XL_CMDLINE="touchscreen=1 cpufreq=1 bootcpu=7 cpus=8 gpu=1 wifi=1 adsp=1" ./xl run
./xl screenshot shot.png
./xl reboot           # back to Android

./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...).

Prebuilt boot image

Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot. It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above).

Building from source

common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest.

  • Kernel — needs theos in ~/theos (cctools and iPhoneOS16.5.sdk) and clang lld python perl. Details: xnu/README.md. 
    xnu/apply.sh && xnu-deps/setup.sh && ./xnu-build.sh -j8 -k
  • Loader — xnuloader/build.sh (clang + lld-link, an EFI application without EDK2).
  • Images — REST=1 userland/build.sh (variables documented at the top of that file).
  • UEFI — uefi/README.md (Project Silicium port); not needed to run, prebuilt/uefi has it.
  • After rebuilding: tools/update-prebuilt.sh refreshes prebuilt/.

Porting to another device

common/new-device.sh <codename> path/to/device.dtb   # profile + loader platform from the phone's device tree

Then follow docs/PORTING.md: the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ (redwood.conf, qemu-virt.conf, _template.conf).

How it works

fastboot boot ──► UEFI (Mu-Silicium) ──► xnuloader (EFI application)
                                           │  stays resident: USB link (fastboot protocol),
                                           │  watchdog, receives the kernel's log
                                           ▼
            XNU (BCM2837 config as the base + our platform)
              ├─ GICv3, timer, video console, return to the loader
              ├─ APFS (images in RAM, iOS volume on flash), ramfs (/private/var, /tmp)
              ├─ minicrypto instead of corecrypto, AMFI and Sandbox stand-ins (MAC policies)
              ├─ driver replacements: IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack
              ├─ input: /dev/redwood-touch ◄─ Goodix GT9916 (phone) / virtio-input (QEMU)
              ├─ GPU: Adreno 642L, Wi-Fi: WCN6750 (ath11k via LinuxKPI), sound: ADSP / virtio-sound
              ▼
   iOS 16.5 launchd → logd, notifyd, cfprefsd, runningboardd, backboardd, SpringBoard, apps
              ├─ our libraries are injected into backboardd, SpringBoard and mediaserverd
              │  (virtual HID services, a few ObjC method swaps — in memory only)
              └─ mediaserverd gets our CoreAudio output device (RedwoodAudio.driver)

The iOS programs, frameworks and dyld shared cache are not changed by a single byte: what they miss is done by the kernel (driver replacements) or by a library the kernel injects with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES (kern.exec_inject).

Layout

Path What
common/ setup.sh (workspace), build.sh / run.sh (per device), new-device.sh, devices/*.conf, ugit
xl drives the phone over USB: loader, kernel runs, logs, screenshots, screen and sound recording
xnuloader/ the loader: loader.c (UEFI application), mkpayload.py (kernel + images + arguments container)
xnu/ our XNU changes: patch, new files, apply.sh / export.sh
xnu-deps/ everything for building XNU on Linux: setup.sh, tool wrappers, stubs
xnu-build.sh, xnu-env.sh kernel build
uefi/, mkxnuimg.py the UEFI port and packing the boot image for fastboot boot
wifi/lx/ the layer on which Linux's Wi-Fi driver builds for our kernel
qemu/ QEMU runs, touch input, screenshots, stack symbolication
tools/ recording (recording.py, sound.py), UFS/flash tools, mk-ath11k.sh, new-workspace.sh, host tests
prebuilt/ built kernel, loader and UEFI pieces (NOTICES.md for the third-party code in the kernel)
docs/ screenshots, checks.md, PORTING.md

Debugging

  • Session log: QEMU's stdout or logs/HHMMSS-run.log from the phone.
  • RC_JOBS=rc.jobs.tour REST=1 userland/build.sh — an image that unlocks and opens every app of the first page.
  • userabort: in the log is the stack of a process that called abort(); usertrap: (with systrace=1) — crashes.
  • Live stacks (QEMU): qemu/touch.py stacks NAME, then qemu/symstack.py LOG NAME (needs ipsw).
  • How a check can lie to you: docs/checks.md.

Screenshots

From the phone's screen, one session (GL=1 REST=1, gpu=1):

Licenses

  • xnu/ is a derivative work of XNU and is distributed under APSL 2.0, like XNU itself; prebuilt/mach.* is the kernel built from it. It also contains ath11k (BSD-3-Clause-Clear) and FreeBSD LinuxKPI code (BSD-2-Clause): see prebuilt/NOTICES.md.
  • xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libzbitmap/ and xnu-deps/build/lzbitmap/ — libzbitmap (Corellium LLC, MIT here); xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libdeflate/ — libdeflate 1.24 (Eric Biggers, MIT, COPYING there).
  • ath11k, Linux and FreeBSD sources are not in the repository: tools/mk-ath11k.sh fetches pinned releases. wifi/lx/patches/*.patch are our changes to FreeBSD headers; the rest of wifi/lx/ is ours.
  • uefi/files/Binaries/redwood and prebuilt/uefi/SILICIUM_UEFI.fd contain UEFI drivers from the phone's Xiaomi firmware, distributed the way Project Silicium distributes them for other devices; prebuilt/uefi/mkbootimg.py — AOSP, Apache-2.0.
  • This repository is licensed under the Apple Public Source License 2.0: our changes to XNU are a derivative of XNU and must be, and our other code here (loader, scripts) is released under the same license. Third-party code keeps its own license, as listed above.

item.title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France (1222 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://quad9.net/news/blog/au-revoir-france/, See on Hacker News

Back to Blog
October 22, 2026 blog

Farewell, France

We have some news to share with you.

Summary

Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.

The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France. 

The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

Background

beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.

Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users. 

We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.

For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way to force users to identify themselves before they can connect to the internet. Our core goals – privacy of user data and honesty of responses - are directly opposed to the methods necessary to implement the blocking this court ruling would require us to perform. There is no way we can determine which users this ruling applies to – we have no list of French users, because we do not keep dossiers of our users at all.

If we do not comply, we will face a daily penalty of 1.000 euros until the blocking concludes on November 14 (i.e., 24.000 euros) not including our legal defense. Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases, nor those of future cases similar to the one brought by beIN. Inaction is, therefore, not an option to challenge this decision.

Can Quad9 just comply via global blocking?

We could add these names to our global malicious domain blocking database, which is what we use to provide internet users with malware and phishing protection. This is a single, monolithic set of names applied to all users of our protective services (9.9.9.9 & secondaries) globally but not to our nonprotective services (9.9.9.10 & secondaries). Blocking these names for all users globally would satisfy the requirements of the court. 

However, this would have the “extraterritorial” effect of applying French legal decisions to every internet user worldwide, when they are meant to solely apply to France, for the commercial benefit of a single private, foreign-owned company. We suspect if other nations wished to impose their national legislation within France, there would be a strong reaction from French users and authorities. The converse is equally true: the findings of a French court are not applicable to the rest of the world. Such a system would set a precedent that any nation could impose their laws, morals, economic demands, or social constructs upon any other nation by the means of blocking DNS names, and thus blocking communication and content. 

Therefore, this global blocking method is entirely unworkable for us as a solution to be compliant with the court order.

What is “France” from the perspective of the internet?

There are more important reasons geoIP blocking will not work. We already prevailed in a similar legal case in Germany in 2021-2023 in which we learned an important lesson: we tried to use geoIP blocking as a “hack” in a similar circumstance at the start of the legal proceedings, allowing us to continue services in Germany until the case concluded. The plaintiff (Sony Music Entertainment GmbH) then used a VPN to access the blocked content from Germany in circumvention of the geoIP blocking. The court agreed with Sony in their assertions of noncompliance, and we were fined for contempt of court. 

From this experience, we know that the geoIP-based model is not only unfit from a technical perspective, but we have proven, historical evidence that using geoIP methods results in fines being levied against us by courts. To any technology-aware person, this seems absurd and outrageous – but this is what we face in these lawsuits where there is a disconnect between the courts’ understanding and how (and why) the technical protocols of the internet actually operate. We cannot risk this negative outcome in this or any other future instance, as absurd decisions apparently are de rigueur in these cases.

We eventually won that case against Sony, but it took several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time – all of which set us back in our ability to deliver services and is a resource debt we are still paying for today. This case is just more of the same – the opposition has more lawyers than we have money and time.

The decision of Quad9

Given these conditions and as a result of our unwavering mission, our historical experience, our desire to remain within the law, and the outcome of the court decision, we are left with an uncomfortable choice.

The demands lead us to an impossible requirement: we must adhere to the court’s decision, or we face growing risks to our existence. However, in implementing the blocking, we must either extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally) or create a vulnerability condition whereby we continue to be at risk because the available technical methods are imprecise,  impossible to validate, and do not meet any user privacy and security requirements.

This leads us to the only conclusion we can understand to eliminate our legal risk and keep us true to our mission: we must make our cybersecurity protection and general services unavailable to French users. Our departure is scheduled for November 24, 2026.

In any event, for Quad9, this is a matter of principle regarding the potential misuse of these types of blocking measures. Allowing private corporations to have the ability to block what is seen on the internet seems to us to be a dangerous and infinitely deep problem. Actions that seem reasonable and infrequent today will tomorrow become an avalanche of petty demands used to suppress political, religious, economic, or social outcomes. We will not be even a small part of that degradation of the freedom of knowledge. Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly.

This case with beIN is not the only litigation we face in France. There are approximately 20 different lawsuits pending against Quad9 (and other recursive resolver operators) that demand we comply with blocking hundreds of different names. We expect many of them to escalate to the same conditions as we have seen with beIN, which puts Quad9 at risk regardless of the outcome of this case. 

Based on the generalized, high-level traffic statistics we keep, we know we have many users in France. With our departure, those users will be put at risk from the threats we have protected them from for nearly 9 years. We deeply regret that result, but we have no other choice. Below is a partial list of the networks from which we see traffic in France. You will see many infrastructure, national security, finance, education, and other networks of critical importance in addition to ISP users and mobile users. All these users will lose service on November 24 because of the legal risks facing Quad9 in France.

What is the purpose of this whole lawsuit, anyway?

The most troubling part of this decision is that it is ineffective in practice. Forcing Quad9 to block domain names does not take the content out of circulation and has no effect on the servers that house the data. 

We offer a free service, and there are thousands of other open DNS systems that do what Quad9 does but with lower trust, safety, and reliability. Users seeking blocked content will simply shift their DNS to use one of those other free services, possibly using systems in other nations that have less-than-honorable intentions from a privacy and security perspective. This is like holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert. It is an unsolvable problem via recursive DNS, and the effect of legal rulings like this is not measurable outside of the amounts paid to lawyers and the number of words in press releases declaring hollow victory. 

Even beIN will not see any changes. Perhaps that is understood and the cruelty may be the point - we cannot say with certainty why such expenditures have been made against a small nonprofit like Quad9, which tries only to bring safer, trusted service to users. But of this we are certain: these actions are a tragic waste of time and resources and create a real, negative outcome for the internet community of France, whether or not they are our users.

What we are doing on November 24

Quad9 will not block the domains in question - we wish to remain committed to our integrity of providing a complete view of the DNS for users who wish that service. However, starting on November 24, we will no longer serve French users, thus keeping Quad9 out of danger from similar, perhaps even larger risks in the future. Our hope is that 30 days will be sufficient time for conversion, though we regret that this message will undoubtedly not reach some users in time.

An appeal is pending, and we will continue to legally defend our position in court in this case and as many other cases as we are able. We will continue to oppose court-ordered DNS blocking of this nature everywhere. Our resources are limited, but we are determined to keep the internet open and free. You can donate here to help us continue to deliver on our mission and assist us in the legal costs we incur in this and other fights.

What you can do next

We think this problem is reversible. French citizens: tell your legislators that looking up names is not a criminal offense. The internet needs to remain open and freely available to anyone, and neutral intermediaries like Quad9 (or any DNS resolver) should not be implicated in legal proceedings because we map names to IP addresses. Further, we know there are potential plans in consideration in France (and other European nations) to give private corporations and others automated and unvalidated abilities to filter DNS content that they alone determine to be unwanted, making it possible for a wide range of badly-managed or anti-democratic activities to be implemented. We believe you disagree with this as much as we do. Make yourself heard, or you will lose your rights silently.

ARCOM is your regulatory authority, and you should tell them this precedent places France at risk both from a practical and strategic perspective. 

Let them know that under their mandate, they have to balance your digital rights as citizens as well as the audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts of rights holders. Balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage.

In conclusion

Fighting piracy via DNS resolvers blocking is ineffective. It is disproportionate and misguided, ill-fitted and futile to fight piracy, as the source content remains completely available to resurge under another name. Forcing Quad9 to depart harms French digital strategy and sovereignty in the long run relating to security, privacy, and integrity - contradicting France’s supreme national interests in exchange for a short-term, imaginary commercial victory.

We deeply regret that we must leave our French users without cybersecurity protection, but we hope the future will see a more reasonable interpretation of the law which allows us to return.

Sincerely,

The Quad9 Team

* This post was authored and translated into French by humans on the Quad9 Team
